title: WAS SODOM DESTROYED ONLY BECAUSE OF SEXUAL SIN? EZEKIEL ADDS DETAILS MANY PEOPLE FORGET
paragraphs: WAS SODOM DESTROYED ONLY BECAUSE OF SEXUAL SIN? EZEKIEL ADDS DETAILS MANY PEOPLE FORGET
We remember what happened behind Sodom’s doors. God also remembered what was happening outside them. And Ezekiel’s description may make the story far more uncomfortable than you expected.
There is something frightening about reading a Bible story for years and suddenly realizing you have been standing safely outside of it.
Sodom.
Just hearing the name can make people think they already know the sermon.
Sexual immorality. Perversion. Judgment. Fire.
And Scripture absolutely does speak about Sodom’s sexual wickedness. We should never erase what the Bible refuses to erase.
But then God says something through Ezekiel that many Christians rarely hear when Sodom is discussed.
Something that moves the spotlight.
Something that takes a story we may have used to point at somebody else...
and turns it toward us.
Listen carefully to the Hebrew of Ezekiel 16:49:
הִנֵּה־זֶה הָיָה עֲוֹן סְדֹם אֲחוֹתֵךְ גָּאוֹן שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם וְשַׁלְוַת הַשְׁקֵט הָיָה לָהּ וְלִבְנוֹתֶיהָ וְיַד־עָנִי וְאֶבְיוֹן לֹא הֶחֱזִיקָה׃
A faithful rendering is essentially:
“Behold, this was the iniquity of your sister Sodom: pride, fullness of bread, and prosperous ease were hers and her daughters’; yet she did not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.”
Then verse 50 continues:
וַתִּגְבְּהֶינָה וַתַּעֲשֶׂינָה תוֹעֵבָה לְפָנָי...
“They became haughty and committed abomination before Me...”
Read that again.
Pride.
Fullness of bread.
Comfort.
Neglect of the poor.
Haughtiness.
Abomination.
And judgment.
Suddenly Sodom feels closer.
Because it is easy to condemn a sin you believe belongs to somebody else.
It is much harder when God starts talking about the sins that can live comfortably in respectable houses.
The Hebrew word translated “pride” is גָּאוֹן — ga'on. It carries the sense of exaltation, arrogance, majesty, pride.
Then comes an expression almost painfully vivid:
שִׂבְעַת־לֶחֶם — siv'at-lechem.
Fullness of bread.
They had enough.
More than enough.
Their stomachs were full while someone else's hands were empty.
And God noticed.
Not because possessing food is sinful.
Not because prosperity automatically makes someone wicked.
Abraham himself possessed great wealth.
The problem was what abundance had done to their hearts.
Their blessings had become insulation.
Their comfort had stopped producing gratitude and started producing indifference.
Their abundance had become an excuse not to see suffering.
They had bread...
but no mercy.
They had ease...
but no compassion.
They had resources...
but would not strengthen the hand of the poor and needy.
And perhaps this is where the ancient ruins of Sodom begin appearing uncomfortably close to our own front doors.
We can have refrigerators full of food and hearts empty of compassion.
We can spend without thinking on things we barely need while calculating whether generosity is worth the inconvenience.
We can sing, “Lord, I love You,” on Sunday and spend Monday protecting a lifestyle in which nobody else's pain is allowed to interrupt us.
We can know theology...
quote Scripture...
debate morality...
and still walk past Lazarus at the gate.
That should disturb us.
But we also need to be extremely careful here, because another error has become common.
Some people quote Ezekiel 16:49 and conclude:
“See? Sodom had nothing to do with sexual sin. It was only about pride and neglecting the poor.”
That is not what the whole Bible says either.
We do not honor Scripture by correcting one oversimplification with another.

Genesis 19 presents a horrifying scene in which the men of Sodom surround Lot's house and demand access to his male visitors. The episode involves attempted sexual violence, degrading lust, brutality, and a terrifying collapse of moral restraint.
And the New Testament does not permit us to remove sexual immorality from Sodom's indictment.
Jude 7 says:
ὡς Σόδομα καὶ Γόμορρα... ἐκπορνεύσασαι καὶ ἀπελθοῦσαι ὀπίσω σαρκὸς ἑτέρας...
The crucial word ἐκπορνεύσασαι — ekporneusasai comes from a verb describing giving oneself over to sexual immorality.
Jude therefore explicitly remembers Sodom and Gomorrah in connection with sexual immorality and pursuing “other/strange flesh.”
So was Sodom destroyed only because of sexual sin?
No.
Was sexual wickedness irrelevant to Sodom's judgment?
Also no.
The biblical picture is larger...
and more terrifying.
Sodom had become a culture of rebellion.
Sexual corruption was part of it.
Pride was part of it.
Violence was part of it.
Abundance without compassion was part of it.
Haughtiness before God was part of it.
Neglect of vulnerable people was part of it.
What happened in Genesis 19 was not some isolated accident occurring in an otherwise compassionate society.
It was fruit growing from a diseased tree.
And Ezekiel takes us toward the roots.
Pride.
Self-satisfaction.
Indifference.
Haughtiness.
Abomination.
A society so consumed with itself that other human beings could become objects to exploit rather than neighbors to love.
And now comes the part we would rather avoid.
Ezekiel was not primarily preaching a sermon so Jerusalem could feel morally superior to Sodom.
He was confronting Jerusalem.
God calls Sodom Jerusalem's “sister” in this prophetic indictment and tells His covenant people that their own wickedness had become so terrible that comparison with Sodom should humiliate them.
Think about that.
The name “Sodom” was not handed to Jerusalem as ammunition.
It was handed to Jerusalem as a mirror.
That changes how Christians should read this passage.
Before asking, “Who in today's culture reminds me of Sodom?”
perhaps we should ask:
“Jesus... where is Sodom hiding in me?”
Where has pride survived beneath Christian vocabulary?
Where have I become comfortable enough that somebody else's suffering feels inconvenient?
Where do I secretly believe my morality makes me superior to people trapped in sins different from mine?
Where am I sexually compromising while maintaining a religious appearance?
Where have lust, pornography, fantasy, adultery, fornication, exploitation, or secret impurity been given a locked room inside my life?
Where have money and comfort become masters?
Where do I have fullness of bread while refusing to strengthen the hand of someone in need?
Where do I condemn publicly what I tolerate privately?
That is where this passage stops being an argument.
It becomes an examination.
And maybe somebody reading this just became uncomfortable.
Good.
Not because shame is the destination.
Because sometimes discomfort is mercy knocking before destruction has to.
The Gospel does not begin by telling us that everybody else is worse.
It tells us the truth about us.
“All have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).
All.
The sexually immoral need Jesus.
The greedy need Jesus.
The proud need Jesus.
The self-righteous need Jesus.
The religious hypocrite needs Jesus.
The person neglecting the poor needs Jesus.
The person drowning in secret lust needs Jesus.
The person who has never committed the scandalous sins everybody whispers about still needs Jesus.
Because the dividing line of the Gospel is not respectable people on one side and scandalous people on the other.
It is sinners...
and a Savior.
And this is where Sodom's warning must lead us—not into smugness, but toward the cross.
Because if we stop at judgment, we have not yet reached the center of Christianity.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to give sinners better behavior.
He came to save sinners.
At Calvary, the holy Son of God bore sin's judgment.
The One who never surrendered to lust...
never exploited the vulnerable...
never ignored the suffering...
never worshiped comfort...
never lied...
never sinned...
was crucified among sinners.
Jesus did not excuse sin.
He carried its penalty.
Grace is not God pretending rebellion does not matter.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that Christ died.
But look again.
You mattered enough that He came.
That is the scandal of grace.
The Gospel does not tell the sexually broken, “Clean yourself up enough and maybe Jesus will receive you.”
It says come to Christ.
Repent.
Believe.
Bring the darkness into His light.
The Gospel does not tell the proud Christian, “At least you are better than those people.”
It says come down from the throne you built for yourself.
Repent.
The Gospel does not tell the prosperous believer that having possessions automatically condemns them.
It asks something far more searching:
Do your possessions possess you?
Has the mercy God poured into your life begun flowing through you?
Can you see the poor?
Can you see the lonely?
Can you see the hungry?
Can you see the person everybody else avoids?
Can you see the sinner without treating their sin lightly or treating them as less human?
Because Jesus could look at sinners with astonishing tenderness without ever calling darkness light.
That is the balance we desperately need.
Truth without cruelty.
Compassion without compromise.
Holiness without self-righteousness.
Grace without pretending repentance is unnecessary.
Jesus embodied all of it.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years thinking their scandal disqualified them from ever becoming useful to God again.
Maybe your Sodom is not theoretical.
Maybe you have lived through sexual sin.
Maybe adultery destroyed your marriage.
Maybe pornography has chained you in secrecy.
Maybe greed hardened you.
Maybe pride destroyed relationships.
Maybe you ignored people God repeatedly placed in your path.
Maybe you have been the religious person throwing stones while carefully hiding what nobody was allowed to discover.
Maybe you know exactly what it feels like to wonder:
“If people knew everything about me, would anybody still love me?”
Jesus already knows.
Every room.
Every browser history.
Every thought.
Every compromise.
Every selfish decision.
Every tear.
Every excuse.
Every secret.
And the Gospel invitation still stands.
Not an invitation to remain unchanged.
An invitation to repent and be made new.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).
That promise does not belong to people who successfully constructed an innocent past.
It belongs to people who are in Christ.
That means your history does not have to become your identity.
Your worst night does not have to write your final chapter.
Your secret does not have to become your tombstone.
Your sin may explain part of your story...
but Jesus Christ can determine its ending.
This is why repentance is not God's attempt to humiliate you.
Repentance is the doorway out of the burning house.
When Christ says turn, He is not trying to rob you of life.
He is calling you back to it.
And maybe that is what Ezekiel's forgotten description of Sodom was supposed to do all along.
Not give us another weapon for culture wars.
Give us a mirror.
Look into it.
Not at your neighbor.
Not at the politician you despise.
Not at the denomination you criticize.
Not at the person whose sexuality you condemn.
Not at the unbeliever whose lifestyle troubles you.
Look at yourself.
Has pride entered?
Has abundance anesthetized compassion?
Has ease made obedience inconvenient?
Has sexual compromise become normalized?
Have you become better at identifying abomination in others than rebellion in yourself?
Have you been fed spiritually for years while refusing to strengthen somebody weaker?
Be honest.
This may have hit harder than you expected.
Tell the truth.
Or simply write:
Not because typing words saves anyone.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes confession begins when somebody finally stops pretending.
Someone else reading those words may realize they are not fighting alone.
And please hear this carefully.
A seeker.
A lukewarm Christian.
Even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to offer except condemnation.
Let them encounter the Christ who tells the truth about sin and then stretches scarred hands toward sinners.
Because temptation has a strange way of making yesterday's conviction disappear tomorrow.
Come back when pride whispers.
Come back when comfort makes you numb.
Come back when lust starts negotiating.
Come back when self-righteousness makes somebody else's sin look enormous and yours look microscopic.
Come back and remember:
Sodom is easier to condemn from a distance than to recognize in a mirror.

And if Gospel Warrior has been helping you return to Scripture, grow deeper in Christ, confront hidden sin, understand difficult passages, and remember the Gospel when your soul is exhausted, stay close.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never will.
It should not.
Give voluntarily, prayerfully, and cheerfully—not under compulsion (see 2 Corinthians 9:7).
Supporting faithful Gospel work can be one meaningful way to use what God has entrusted to you for His glory—but glorifying God is never something you purchase.
you can still help.
That costs nothing.
You may never know who reads because you shared.
You may never see the person crying behind a phone screen.
You may never know whose secret sin was confronted.
Whose hardened heart softened.
Whose faith awakened.
Whose shame finally drove them toward Christ instead of farther into hiding.
Gospel Warrior cannot save anyone.
An article cannot save anyone.
A church cannot save anyone.
A Christian product cannot save anyone.
Jesus Christ saves.
That is why everything must return to Him.
Sodom reminds us that God takes sexual sin seriously.
Ezekiel reminds us that He also takes pride, abundance without mercy, haughtiness, complacency, and neglect of the poor seriously.
Jude prevents us from rewriting the story as though sexual immorality played no role at all.
And the Gospel prevents us from reading any of this merely to discover whom we are allowed to condemn.
The cross levels us.
At its foot stands the sexually broken.
The greedy.
The arrogant.
The wounded.
The hypocrite.
The addict.
The religious.
The irreligious.
The rich.
The poor.
The ashamed.
The person everyone knows has sinned...
and the person whose scandal has never been discovered.
All empty-handed.
All unable to purchase mercy.
All needing the same Savior.
And there...
where judgment and mercy meet...
Jesus rewrites stories.
Maybe yours is next.
So repent where you need to repent.
Forgive where Christ commands you to forgive.
Make restitution where righteousness requires it.
Break with the secret sin you have been protecting.
Open your hand to the needy.
Come down from pride.
Stop calling comfort peace when it has actually become spiritual sleep.
And run to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not after you become respectable.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Now.
Because the deepest warning in Sodom's story may not merely be that terrible sinners can face judgment.
It may be that people can become so comfortable with darkness that eventually they stop recognizing darkness at all.
But the breathtaking promise of the Gospel is this:
Christ still calls sinners out of darkness.
And when He calls...
the proper response is not to defend the darkness.
It is to walk toward the Light.
Then send this to somebody whose story looks too broken to be rewritten.
Because somewhere tonight, someone believes their scandal is the end of their story.
May they discover that the ashes do not get the final word when Jesus holds the pen.
